gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the only single-store whole-home battery + generator cart on an approved store is Anker SOLIX's E10 (1× Power Module + 2× Battery) + Power Dock + Smart Generator 5500 bundle at $9,399. It is $399 less than buying the parts separately, and it pairs the battery with the one generator that charges it over a 4,500 W DC cable and starts itself at a set battery level. A third-party portable generator on 120 V charges the E10 at only 1,800 W, and only a 240 V standby generator with two-wire or utility-sensing control can be auto-started.
standout_why: I compared against the cited FranklinWH pages: 'Can I use a generator with my FranklinWH system?', the Generator Module page and the aPower 2 page. They say that a portable or standby generator works, that it can auto-start at a set battery level, and that it should have clean output. They give no charging power, no 120 V vs 240 V difference, no auto-start requirement such as two-wire control, no price and no buyable cart, because FranklinWH is sold only through installers. The SOC auto-start idea is already on the FranklinWH Generator Module page. What is new is the 4,500 W DC vs 1,800 W (120 V AC) charge-rate gap, the rule that a third-party generator needs two-wire control to auto-start, and that the bundle is $399 less than the parts bought separately.
kit_items: Home battery + inverter: Anker SOLIX E10 (1× Power Module + 2× B6000 Battery), 12 kWh, ≤20 ms switchover. It is the only whole-home battery on an approved store whose maker also sells a matching generator in the same cart.
Transfer / source hub: Anker SOLIX Power Dock. It links grid, solar and generator, and it is what lets the E10 start a standby generator when the battery drops to the level you set.

Generator: Anker SOLIX Smart Generator 5500 (Tri-Fuel: gasoline, LPG or natural gas). It connects to the E10 over a dedicated 4,500 W DC power-and-communication cable and auto-starts by battery state of charge. A 120 V portable generator charges the E10 at 1,800 W at most.

findings.product: Anker SOLIX E10 with a third-party generator
findings.label: AC charge limit and auto-start requirement
findings.value: Up to 1,800 W charging on 120 V; up to 7,680 W on 240 V; E10 AC Generator Adapter bypass up to 9,600 W; auto-start only with a 240 V standby generator that has Two Wire or Utility Sensing control, max 24 kW surge; THD below 10%
findings.source_title: Automatic Generator Integration for Home Battery – Anker SOLIX blog
findings.note: The blog says 'most portable models lack SOC-based or app-controlled auto-start'. So a 120 V portable charges at 1,800 W, which is 40% of the Smart Generator 5500's 4,500 W DC path, and it gets no auto-start.

findings.label: What the cited rival states
findings.value: Portable or standby generator; auto-start at a customer-set SOC, scheduled or manual; clean inverter output; no kW figures, no price
findings.note: I also read https://www.franklinwh.com/support/articles/detail/can-i-use-a-generator-with-my-franklinwh-system. It has no charging power figures and no 2-wire or transfer-switch detail.
